chapter_theme: The last two couplets of the Puranamalai: the confession is summed up as having wandered in a void at the bottom instead of completing and seeing the void at the end, and the garland closes with its promise, that the Fullness will make knowledge flourish on earth for those who recite the Puranamalai with understanding.
structure_note: 774 belongs with the confessions of the preceding chapter and 775 is the work's phala-sruti; the tool's five-way split leaves them as a chapter of two verses.

774.reading: Instead of standing at the end, bringing one void to its completion and looking, I wandered in a void at the bottom.
774.nuance: The verse uses சூனியம், the Siddhars' Buddhist-flavoured word for the void, twice, and the reading turns on which void is which. On the plain reading the void at the end (முடிவில்) is the emptiness in which the Fullness is seen, reached by completing the path, and the void at the bottom (அடியில்) is the empty world, or the nothing one wanders in without the path. Tradition also reads அடி and முடி as the foot and the crown of the body, the base centre and the summit of the yogic ascent, so that the poet confesses having circled at the base rather than finishing at the crown. Either way the verse admits two voids, a true and a false, and does not say what distinguishes them beyond their place.

775.reading: For those who recite this Puranamalai with understanding you will make knowledge flourish on this earth.
775.nuance: A phala-sruti, the conventional closing promise, but conditioned on புத்தியுடன், with understanding, which answers the garland's opening charge of mouth-knowledge (749): recitation alone is what the poem has been attacking, so the fruit is withheld from it. தாரணியில், on the earth, places the promised knowledge in this life.

links.note: Tirumular takes the void as his way, crosses it, and comes to rest in the void that has shaken off even that imagining; Pattinathar distinguishes the void at the end, which is completed and seen, from the void at the bottom, in which he wandered. Both hold that there are two voids, one to be passed through or left and one to be reached, and that mistaking the first for the second is the failure.

source_issues: The tool's division of the Puranamalai into five chapters cuts 774 off from the confessions of 755 to 773 and leaves this chapter with two verses.
